title: What is the Most Effective Teaching Sequence?
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Dominic Salles takes the popular I do, We do, You do structure and argues it is good but incomplete. Drawing on an extract from his book, he says it quietly assumes the teacher must model live, when a prepared model is more exact and spares every teacher the load. It also leaves misconceptions unaddressed. His fix is See, Try, Apply, Secure: a prepared model, a paired attempt, an application task, and a final teacher-designed phase that exposes and corrects remaining misconceptions. He closes by arguing that new teachers learn to plan best by imitating well-planned shared units rather than planning alone from scratch.
points: I do, We do, You do omits a paired-practice step and a final misconception-checking step.
Prepared models are more precise than live ones and reduce teacher cognitive load across a department.
Paired work lets the teacher spot the misconceptions that most need whole-class correction in minutes.
Novice teachers should learn to plan by studying and imitating strong shared units, not by planning individually.
quotes: This really matters - things that appear common sense in your first 10 years of teaching can appear hopelessly ineffective once you pass that 10,000 hour threshold.

First, the I do also implies that learning is best when the teacher live models with the students. Notice in my example, the model was already written. This means there is much less cognitive load for the teacher, and it also means that the model is likely to be more exact and concise, because it has been prepared in advance. When we look at the centralised curriculum, you’ll also see that it has the added merit of liberating every teacher from having to write the model live, not just you.
To overcome their misconceptions, we need a step before the you do, and a further step after it. You can see the further step with the visualiser and steps 10 and 11 in the sequence above.
Having wandered past 8 pairs in the space of a minute or two you will know exactly which misconceptions are most necessary for the whole class to have corrected before they move on to the I do.

Secure is an I do activity. It forces you to design a series of further activities which will identify student misconceptions, and give them at least one further attempt to improve. This will dramatically increase their progress – we might as much as double it for a student who has struggled with the I do phase of the earlier teaching sequence.

You can’t practise what you don’t know, not deliberately anyway. The stupidity of being forced to plan before you fully understand what good learning and planning looks like is responsible for a very high dropout rate of trainee and new teachers, causes huge stress for those who persevere, and dramatically slows progress once you start in the profession.
The hardest part is deciding what you want students to learn. Then you make sure each activity is devoted to that.
